```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[sort.Ints] --> SS[sort.Slice: any type, any less]
    SS --> ST[sort.SliceStable: equal elements keep order]
    G[slices.Sort: generics, natural ordering]
    G --> SF[slices.SortFunc: by comparison]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The algorithm underneath: Go's sort uses pdqsort (pattern-defeating quicksort, Go 1.19+) — a hybrid (quicksort, insertion-sort for small ranges, heapsort as the fallback to avoid quicksort's O(n²) worst case). The pdqsort innovation: pattern detection (already-sorted runs, reverse-sorted runs) — beating the naive cases that plague plain quicksort.

The stability distinction in practice: users sorted by Age — two users with the same Age: sort.Slice may reorder them; sort.SliceStable preserves their original order. The practical impact: when the data has a prior order (a secondary sort key), the stable form composes the keys (sort by name first, then stable-sort by age — the name order survives within ages).

The slices package's significance (1.21+): generics enable the natural-ordering form (slices.Sort on any cmp.Ordered element) — no more Less functions for the common case. The ecosystem is migrating; the sort package remains forever — the two coexist.
